title: The abbot is invited
hookLine: King Trisong Detsen invites the Indian abbot Shantarakshita

lines: A KING CAN'T BUILD A TEACHER.
cards: A king can build a temple. He can't build a teacher.
Later in Tibet's story, another king, Trisong Detsen, wanted the Buddha's teaching to take real root in his land: not only images in temples, but monks, study and practice.
For that he needed someone who knew it from the inside. So he did what a king can do. He sent an invitation over the Himalaya, to India.

teach.b: The man invited was Shantarakshita, a learned Indian abbot and a philosopher in his own right. Tibetans remember him as the great abbot.
He came, and taught the foundations: avoid harm, do good, see how actions bring their results. Then trouble came too.
The Tibetan accounts tell of floods, lightning and sickness, and of people who said the old gods of the land were angry at the newcomer. Some at court opposed the new teaching outright.

Here the abbot did something worth noticing. He didn't insist he was enough. Tradition says he told the king that this work needed a different kind of teacher, one who could meet those forces head on, and he named him.
The abbot stepped back to make room.
Count the invitations in this stretch of the story. A queen comes from Nepal and a queen from China. A king invites an abbot.
The abbot asks the king to invite someone else. The teaching doesn't march in.
It is asked in, and then it asks for help.

That's this whole week, too: the great Buddha of Nara, Mount Hiei and Mount Koya, new schools for ordinary people, practice spilling into tea and ink, then Tibet, where two queens carried the Buddha in.
Again and again, someone asks, or is asked. Tomorrow, the one the abbot named.

how: Tibetan Buddhists honor Shantarakshita, Padmasambhava and King Trisong Detsen together as founders of the teaching in Tibet, and it is customary for students to formally request teachings before a teacher gives them.

practice: Bring to mind one question you've been carrying alone, and one person who might know more about it, a teacher, an elder, a friend who's been through it.
Picture asking them, and notice whatever makes asking hard without obeying it; if you pray, you can ask for help in finding the right person.
